claims.text: Chemical dealloying can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks in noble metal–based high-entropy alloys.
Chemical dealloying selectively dissolves less-noble or sacrificial elements from an NM-HEA precursor.
Selective dissolution leaves an interconnected, porous, noble metal–rich structure.
The proposed precursor is a bulk NM-HEA containing highly noble and less-noble elements in near-equiatomic proportions.
Controlled acid etching can preferentially remove the more dissolvable elements from the alloy.
Control of acid concentration, temperature, and etching time can favor preferential dissolution while preserving the high-entropy framework.
Selective element dissolution triggers formation of a bicontinuous three-dimensional porous structure.
The remaining noble metals reconfigure into a nanoframework during dealloying.
The dealloying mechanism depends on disparities in chemical stability among the constituent elements.
Less-noble sacrificial components dissolve faster than the retained components during dealloying.
The remaining metals reorganize into an interconnected network with high surface area.
The resulting nanoframework has enhanced surface area and potential catalytic sites.
The nanoframework may improve catalytic performance relative to the as-cast precursor.
Effective dealloying requires a sufficient difference in electrochemical stability between alloying elements.
Overly aggressive dealloying may cause complete loss of structural integrity.
Conditions that are too mild may fail to produce a well-defined nanoframework.
Precise control of pore size, ligament distribution, and nanostructural uniformity is challenging and requires process optimization.
Residual stress and elemental reordering during dealloying may affect catalytic properties.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome treats improved catalytic performance as only a possibility, but the falsification rule states that failure to improve catalytic performance can falsify the nanoframework-production hypothesis. This makes an optional downstream benefit an overly strong requirement for the core structural claim.
